Hubert Flenner Address: Fakultät für Mathematik, Ruhr Universität Bochum, Geb. NA 2/72, Universitätsstr. 150, 44780 Bochum, Germany Email address: Hubert.Flenner@ruhr-uni-bochum.de and Mikhail Zaidenberg Address: Université Grenoble I, Institut Fourier, UMR 5582 CNRS-UJF, BP 74, 38402 St. Martin d’Hères cédex, France Email address: zaidenbe@ujf-grenoble.fr
Abstract.

It is an open question whether every normal affine surface VV over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} admits an effective action of a maximal torus 𝕋=ℂ∗n{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{C}}^{*n} (n≤2n\leq 2) such that any other effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action is conjugate to a subtorus of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} in Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V). We prove that this holds indeed in the following cases: (a) the Makar-Limanov invariant ML⁡(V)≠ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(V)\neq{\mathbb{C}} is nontrivial, (b) VV is a toric surface, (c) V=ℙ1×ℙ1\ΔV={\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta, where Δ\Delta is the diagonal, and (d) V=ℙ2\QV={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q, where QQ is a nonsingular quadric. In case (a) this generalizes a result of Bertin for smooth surfaces, whereas (b) was previously known for the case of the affine plane (Gutwirth [Gut]) and (d) is a result of Danilov-Gizatullin [DG] and Doebeli [Do].

1. Introduction

The classification problem for reductive group actions on affine spaces or, more generally, on affine varieties, has a long history. By [Kam, KP, KKMR, Po] any reductive group action on 𝔸ℂ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}} and 𝔸ℂ3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}} is conjugate to a linear one. The same holds for connected reductive groups acting on 𝔸ℂ4{\mathbb{A}}^{4}_{\mathbb{C}} except possibly for ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} and ℂ∗2{\mathbb{C}}^{*2} [Pa, Po] (cf. also [BaHab]), and for tori 𝕋n{\mathbb{T}}^{n} acting effectively on 𝔸ℂn{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, 𝔸ℂn+1{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1} [BB] and on the affine toric nn-folds [De, Gub]. According to [Sc, MMP, Kn] many finite nonabelian groups and any connected reductive nonabelian group admit a non-linearizable action on some affine space 𝔸ℂn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}. In the local case the existence of a maximal reductive subgroup of Aut⁡(V,0){\operatorname{Aut}}(V,0), which contains a conjugate of any other connected reductive subgroup, was established in [HM]. In [DG, Do] the same was shown to be true for the smooth affine quadric surface in 𝔸ℂ3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}}. It is an open question whether this holds as well for every normal affine surface VV. In this paper we give some partial positive results, see Corollary 5.5 below.

Bertin’s Theorem [Be, Corollary 2.3] asserts that, for a smooth affine surface VV non-isomorphic to ℂ∗×ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, which admits a minimal compactification VV by a simple normal crossing divisor DD with a non-linear dual graph ΓD\Gamma_{D}, any two effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on VV are conjugated in the automorphism group Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V). On the other hand, by Gizatullin’s Theorem [Gi, Theorems 2 and 3] (see also [BML, Be] or [Du] for the more general case of normal surfaces), if V≇𝔸ℂ1×ℂ∗V\not\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} then ΓD\Gamma_{D} is linear if and only if the Makar-Limanov invariant

ML(V):=⋂∂∈LND⁡(A)ker∂{\operatorname{ML}}(V):=\bigcap_{{\partial}\in{\operatorname{LND}}(A)}\ker{\partial}

of VV is trivial that is, ML⁡(V)=ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(V)={\mathbb{C}}, where LND⁡(A){\operatorname{LND}}(A) stands for the set of all locally nilpotent derivations of the coordinate ring A=H0​(V,𝒪V)A=H^{0}(V,{\mathcal{O}}_{V}) of VV. The latter holds if and only if VV admits two non-equivalent effective ℂ+{\mathbb{C}}_{+}-actions i.e., two ℂ+{\mathbb{C}}_{+}-actions with different general orbits (see e.g., [FZ2]).

We present here an alternative proof of Bertin’s Theorem, valid more generally for normal affine surfaces. Our proof is not based on the properties of completions and so is independent of Gizatullin’s Theorem. In Theorem 3.3 below we show that, as soon as ML⁡(V)≠ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(V)\neq{\mathbb{C}} and V≇ℂ∗×ℂ∗V\not\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} or 𝔸ℂ1×ℂ∗{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, any two effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on VV are conjugated via an element of a ℂ+{\mathbb{C}}_{+}-subgroup of the automorphism group Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V).

For a surface VV with an effective action of the 2-torus 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} we prove in Theorem 4.5 that any effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action on VV is conjugated in Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) to the action of a subtorus of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}. In the case of the affine plane V=𝔸ℂ2V={\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{2} this gives another proof of the classical Gutwirth Theorem [Gut] saying that the linearization conjecture for ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on 𝔸ℂn{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{n} holds in dimension 2.

In Section 5 we deduce similar results for the surfaces ℙ1×ℙ1\Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta and ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q, where Δ\Delta is the diagonal in ℙ1×ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and QQ is a nonsingular quadric in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. We show that any two effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on one of these surfaces are conjugate in the automorphism group. According to a result of Gizatullin and Popov (see [FZ2, Theorem 4.12]) these are the only normal affine surfaces that admit a nontrivial 𝐒𝐋2{\bf{SL}}_{2}-action except for the affine plane and the affine Veronese cones over the rational normal curves. We note that by [FZ2, Proposition 4.14] any two 𝐒𝐋2{\bf{SL}}_{2}-actions on a normal affine surface are conjugate in the automorphism group.

Our interest in such kind of results is related with our studies [FZ1, FZ2] on the Dolgachev-Pinkham-Demazure (or DPD, for short) presentation of a normal affine surface VV endowed with a ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action. We show in Corollary 4.3 that for surfaces with a non-trivial Makar-Limanov invariant, except in the case of the surfaces ℂ∗×ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} and 𝔸C1×ℂ∗{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{C}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, this DPD-presentation is uniquely determined up to a natural equivalence. For affine toric surfaces we describe in Section 4 the possible ambiguities in the choice of a DPD-presentation. We also deduce the uniqueness of the DPD-presentation for the surfaces ℙ1×ℙ1\Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta and ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q as above, which are non-toric and have a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant.

In Corollary 5.5 we deduce that all maximal connected reductive subgroups of the automorphism group Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) are conjugate, and any connected reductive subgroup is contained in a maximal one, besides the remaining open case when the surface is non-toric and has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant. In the forthcoming paper [FKZ] we will solve this remaining case, up to one exception, by showing that the automorphism group Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) contains a unique class of conjugated ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-subgroups, which also implies the uniqueness of a DPD-presentation up to a natural equivalence.

2. Preliminaries

Let kk be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 00. We recall the following definition.

Definition 2.1.

Let AA be a kk-algebra, not necessarily associative or commutative. A derivation δ:A→A\delta:A\to A is called locally bounded if every finite subset of AA is contained in some δ\delta-invariant linear subspace V⊆AV\subseteq A of finite dimension over kk.

For instance, if δ:A→A\delta:A\to A is a semisimple derivation on AA i.e., AA has a kk-basis consisting of eigenvectors of δ\delta then δ\delta is locally bounded.

Clearly if δ\delta is locally bounded then AA is the union of its finite dimensional δ\delta-invariant subspaces VV. In particular, the restriction of δ\delta to each such subspace VV admits a unique Jordan-Chevalley decomposition

δ=δs+δn,\delta=\delta_{s}+\delta_{n},

where δs\delta_{s} and δn\delta_{n} are the semisimple and the nilpotent parts of δ\delta, respectively. The restriction to a smaller δ\delta-invariant subspace respects this decomposition, hence δs\delta_{s} and δn\delta_{n} are well-defined kk-linear maps on AA that are again locally bounded. We will see in Lemma 2.2 below that these maps are as well derivations on AA.

For α∈k\alpha\in k we consider the linear subspace

Aα:=⋃i≥0ker⁡(δ−α​id)i.A_{\alpha}:=\bigcup_{i\geq 0}\ker(\delta-\alpha\operatorname{id})^{i}\,.

From standard linear algebra we know that

V=⨁α(V∩Aα),V=\bigoplus_{\alpha}(V\cap A_{\alpha})\,,

whenever VV is a finite dimensional δ\delta-invariant subspace of AA. Thus AA is a graded vector space

A=⨁α∈kAα.A=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in k}A_{\alpha}\,.

Clearly, δs\delta_{s} and δn\delta_{n} leave invariant every subspace AαA_{\alpha}. Moreover δs\delta_{s} acts on AαA_{\alpha} via multiplication by α\alpha, whereas δn|Aα\delta_{n}|A_{\alpha} is locally nilpotent. More precisely, we have the following lemma (see e.g., [Ch, Thm. 16] or [Ja, Ch. II, Ex. 8] for the case of algebras of finite dimension, [SW] for complete algebras, and also [CD, 2.1]).

Lemma 2.2.
  1. (a)

    AA is a graded algebra, i.e. Aα​Aβ⊆Aα+βA_{\alpha}A_{\beta}\subseteq A_{\alpha+\beta} for all α\alpha, β∈k\beta\in k;

  2. (b)

    δs\delta_{s} and δn\delta_{n} are again derivations on AA;

  3. (c)

    δs\delta_{s} is homogeneous and acts on AαA_{\alpha} via multiplication by α\alpha, so is automatically locally bounded, whereas δn\delta_{n} is homogeneous of degree 00 and locally nilpotent.

Proof.

(a) For homogeneous elements x∈Aαx\in A_{\alpha} and y∈Aβy\in A_{\beta} we have

(δ−(α+β)​id)​(x​y)=x⁡(δ−β​id)​(y)+(δ−α​id)​(x)​y,(\delta-(\alpha+\beta)\operatorname{id})(xy)=x(\delta-\beta\operatorname{id})(y)+(\delta-\alpha\operatorname{id})(x)y\,,

and hence by induction

(δ−(α+β)​id)n​(x​y)=∑i=0n(ni)​(δ−α​id)i​(x)⋅(δ−β​id)n−i​(y).(\delta-(\alpha+\beta)\operatorname{id})^{n}(xy)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}{n\choose i}(\delta-\alpha\operatorname{id})^{i}(x)\cdot(\delta-\beta\operatorname{id})^{n-i}(y)\,.

It follows that (δ−(α+β)​id)n​(x​y)(\delta-(\alpha+\beta)\operatorname{id})^{n}(xy) vanishes for n≫0n\gg 0, and so x​y∈Aα+βxy\in A_{\alpha+\beta}, proving (a).

By definition δs\delta_{s} acts via multiplication with α\alpha on AαA_{\alpha}. Since AA is a graded algebra this shows that δs\delta_{s} is a degree 00 homogeneous derivation on AA and so is δn=δ−δs\delta_{n}=\delta-\delta_{s}. Now (b) and (c) follow. ∎

In the next lemma we consider the set

M:={α∈k|Aα≠0},M:=\{\alpha\in k|A_{\alpha}\neq 0\}\,,

and we let ℕ​M{\mathbb{N}}M and ℤ​M{\mathbb{Z}}M be the additive subsemigroup and the subgroup of kk, respectively, generated by MM.

Lemma 2.3.

If AA is a finitely generated kk-algebra then

  1. (a)

    also ℕ​M{\mathbb{N}}M and ℤ​M{\mathbb{Z}}M are finitely generated, and

  2. (b)

    AA admits an effective action of a torus (k∗)r(k^{*})^{r}, where r:=rkℤ⁡ℤ​Mr:={\operatorname{rk}}_{\mathbb{Z}}{\mathbb{Z}}M.

Proof.

The proof of (a) is elementary and we omit it. To show (b) we note that A=⨁α∈MAαA=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in M}A_{\alpha} is graded by the semigroup ℕ​M{\mathbb{N}}M, which is a subsemigroup of ℤ​M≅ℤr{\mathbb{Z}}M\cong{\mathbb{Z}}^{r}. An effective action of (k∗)r(k^{*})^{r} on AA is then given by

(λ1,…,λr).xα:=λ1α1⋯λrαrxα,xα∈Aα,(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{r}).x_{\alpha}:=\lambda_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\lambda_{r}^{\alpha_{r}}x_{\alpha},\quad x_{\alpha}\in A_{\alpha},

where (λ1,…,λr)∈(k∗)r(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{r})\in(k^{*})^{r} and α∈M⊆ℤr\alpha\in M\subseteq{\mathbb{Z}}^{r} has components α1,…,αr∈ℤ\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{r}\in{\mathbb{Z}}. ∎

Lemma 2.4.

If ∂:A→A{\partial}:A\to A is a locally nilpotent derivation then

(1) exp(−∂)δexp(∂)=δ+[δ,∂]\displaystyle\exp(-{\partial})\delta\exp({\partial})=\delta+[\delta,{\partial}]

for any derivation δ:A→A\delta:A\to A satisfying

(2) [[δ,∂],∂]=0.\displaystyle[[\delta,{\partial}],{\partial}]=0\,.
Proof.

We denote Δi:=[δ,∂i]\Delta_{i}:=[\delta,{\partial}^{i}]. Then (2) says that [Δ1,∂]=0[\Delta_{1},{\partial}]=0. By the Jacobi identity we get

(3) [Δi,∂]=[Δ1,∂i],\displaystyle[\Delta_{i},{\partial}]=[\Delta_{1},{\partial}^{i}]\,,

and so by (2) [Δi,∂]=0∀i≥1[\Delta_{i},{\partial}]=0\quad\forall i\geq 1.

Assuming by induction that, for a given ii,

(4) Δi=i​∂i−1Δ1,\displaystyle\Delta_{i}=i{\partial}^{i-1}\Delta_{1}\,,

we obtain from the above equalities:

Δi+1=[δ,∂i+1]=Δi∂+∂iΔ1=i∂i−1Δ1∂+∂iΔ1=(i+1)∂iΔ1,\Delta_{i+1}=[\delta,{\partial}^{i+1}]=\Delta_{i}{\partial}+{\partial}^{i}\Delta_{1}=i{\partial}^{i-1}\Delta_{1}{\partial}+{\partial}^{i}\Delta_{1}=(i+1){\partial}^{i}\Delta_{1}\,,

which proves (4) for all i≥1i\geq 1. Thus we get

δ∂i=Δi+∂iδ=∂iδ+i∂i−1Δ1,\delta{\partial}^{i}=\Delta_{i}+{\partial}^{i}\delta={\partial}^{i}\delta+i{\partial}^{i-1}\Delta_{1}\,,

and consequently

δ​exp⁡(∂)=∑i=0∞δ∂i/i!=(∑i=0∞∂i/i!)δ+(∑i=1∞(∂i−1/(i−1)!))Δ1=exp(∂)(δ+[δ,∂]).\begin{array}[]{rcl}\delta\exp({\partial})&=&\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\delta{\partial}^{i}/i!\\ &=&\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{\partial}^{i}/i!\right)\delta+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}({\partial}^{i-1}/(i-1)!)\right)\Delta_{1}\\ &=&\exp({\partial})(\delta+[\delta,{\partial}]).\end{array}

Multiplying with exp(−∂)\exp(-{\partial}) from the left gives (1). ∎

3. Main theorem

In this section we formulate and prove our main results. For any ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded finitely generated ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-algebra

A=⨁i∈ℤAi,A=\bigoplus_{i\in{\mathbb{Z}}}A_{i}\,,

every derivation ∂{\partial} of AA has a unique decomposition ∂=∑i=kl∂i,{\partial}=\sum_{i=k}^{l}{\partial}_{i}\,, where ∂i:A→A{\partial}_{i}:A\to A is a homogeneous derivation of degree ii. The proof of the following simple lemma is left to the reader.

Lemma 3.1.

If ∂=∑i=kl∂i{\partial}=\sum_{i=k}^{l}{\partial}_{i} is locally bounded then ∂l{\partial}_{l} and ∂k{\partial}_{k} are also locally bounded. In particular, if l>0l>0 (k<0k<0) then ∂l{\partial}_{l} (respectively, ∂k{\partial}_{k}) is locally nilpotent.

3.2.

In the sequel we let AA be the coordinate ring of a normal affine surface with a ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action so that A=⨁i∈ℤAiA=\bigoplus_{i\in{\mathbb{Z}}}A_{i} is graded. The infinitesimal generator of this ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action is a semisimple derivation δ\delta on AA that acts via δ⁡(a)=deg⁡(a)⋅a\delta(a)=\deg(a)\cdot a for a homogeneous element a∈Aa\in A. As was shown in [FZ2, Proposition 2.4], for a homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation ∂≠0{\partial}\neq 0 the derivation

exp(−∂)δexp(∂)\exp(-{\partial})\delta\exp({\partial})

is again semisimple and defines a ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action which is, in general, different from the given one. Conversely, we have the following result.

Theorem 3.3.

If ML⁡(A)≠ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(A)\neq{\mathbb{C}}, Spec⁡(A)≇ℂ∗×ℂ∗\operatorname{Spec}(A)\not\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} and ≇𝔸ℂ1×ℂ∗\not\cong{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} then every semisimple derivation δ~{\tilde{\delta}} on AA is of the form

δ~=c⋅exp(−∂)δexp(∂),c∈ℂ,{\tilde{\delta}}=c\cdot\exp(-{\partial})\delta\exp({\partial}),\qquad c\in{\mathbb{C}},

for some locally nilpotent derivation ∂{\partial} on AA. Consequently, any two effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions of AA, after possibly switching one of them by the automorphism λ⟼λ−1\lambda\longmapsto\lambda^{-1} of ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, are conjugate via an automorphism of AA provided by a ℂ+{\mathbb{C}}_{+}-action on AA and, moreover, coincide whenever M​L​(A)=AML(A)=A.

The latter assertion leads to the following corollary.

Corollary 3.4.

If a normal affine surface V=Spec⁡(A)V=\operatorname{Spec}(A), non-isomorphic to ℂ∗×ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, admits two effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions with infinitesimal generators δ,δ~\delta,\tilde{\delta}, where δ≠±δ~\delta\neq\pm\tilde{\delta}, then it also admits a non-trivial ℂ+{\mathbb{C}}_{+}-action.

To prove Theorem 3.3 we need a few preparations.

3.5.

We suppose below that ML⁡(A)≠ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(A)\neq{\mathbb{C}}, Spec⁡(A)≇ℂ∗×ℂ∗\operatorname{Spec}(A)\not\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} and ≇𝔸ℂ1×ℂ∗\not\cong{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}. If AA admits a homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation ∂{\partial} of degree zero then by Lemma 3.8 and Corollary 3.28 in [FZ2] either A≅ℂ⁡[t,u]A\cong{\mathbb{C}}[t,u] or A≅ℂ⁡[t,u,u−1]A\cong{\mathbb{C}}[t,u,u^{-1}] with t∈A0,u∈Adt\in A_{0},u\in A_{d} homogeneous and ∂=∂/∂t{\partial}={\partial}/{\partial}t, which is excluded by our assumptions. According to Corollary 3.27(i) and Theorem 4.5 from [FZ2], either all nontrivial homogeneous locally nilpotent derivations on AA are of positive degree, or all of them are of negative degree. By switching the grading to the opposite one, if necessary, we may suppose in the sequel that AA does not admit a homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation of degree ≤0\leq 0.

Lemma 3.6.

With the assumptions of 3.2 and 3.5, for every nonzero locally nilpotent derivation ∂{\partial} of AA the following hold.

  1. (a)

    ∂{\partial} is a linear combination of commuting homogeneous locally nilpotent derivations of strictly positive degrees.

  2. (b)

    The derivations [δ,∂][\delta,{\partial}] and ∂{\partial} commute.

  3. (c)

    exp(−∂)δexp(∂)=δ+[δ,∂]\exp(-{\partial})\delta\exp({\partial})=\delta+[\delta,{\partial}].

  4. (d)

    There exists a locally nilpotent derivation ∂′{\partial}^{\prime} on AA such that ∂=[δ,∂′]{\partial}=[\delta,{\partial}^{\prime}].

Proof.

(a) Let us write ∂{\partial} as a sum of homogeneous derivations

∂=∑i=kl∂iwith∂k,∂l≠0.{\partial}=\sum_{i=k}^{l}{\partial}_{i}\quad\mbox{with}\quad{\partial}_{k},{\partial}_{l}\neq 0.

Since clearly ∂k{\partial}_{k} and ∂l{\partial}_{l} are again locally nilpotent (see e.g., [Re]), by our convention in 3.5 above we have k≥l>0k\geq l>0. Moreover, since ML⁡(A)≠ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(A)\neq{\mathbb{C}}, ∂{\partial} and ∂k{\partial}_{k} are equivalent, so define equivalent 𝔸ℂ1{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{1}-fibrations, and ∂=a∂l{\partial}=a{\partial}_{l} for some a∈Frac(ker∂l)a\in\operatorname{Frac}(\ker{\partial}_{l}) (see e.g., [FZ2, Lemma 4.5]). It follows that the ∂i{\partial}_{i} are commuting locally nilpotent derivations, proving (a).

Now (b) follows from (a) since [δ,∂]=∑i=kli∂i[\delta,{\partial}]=\sum_{i=k}^{l}i{\partial}_{i}, and (c) follows from Lemma 2.4 by virtue of (b). Finally, (d) can be deduced by taking ∂′:=∑i=kl∂i/i.{\partial}^{\prime}:=\sum_{i=k}^{l}{\partial}_{i}/i. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.3.

For a semisimple derivation δ~{\tilde{\delta}} of AA, we consider its decomposition δ~=∑i=kl∂i{\tilde{\delta}}=\sum_{i=k}^{l}{\partial}_{i} into homogeneous components with ∂k{\partial}_{k}, ∂l≠0{\partial}_{l}\neq 0. By Lemma 3.1, if k<0k<0 then ∂k{\partial}_{k} is locally nilpotent, which is excluded by our convention in 3.5. Thus l≥k≥0l\geq k\geq 0.

Now the proof proceeds by induction on ll. If l=0l=0 then δ~=∂0{\tilde{\delta}}={\partial}_{0} is semisimple, homogeneous of degree 0 and commutes with δ\delta. Thus δ\delta and ∂0{\partial}_{0} are equal up to a constant factor. Indeed, otherwise V:=Spec⁡(A)V:=\operatorname{Spec}(A) would be a toric surface non-isomorphic to ℂ∗×ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} or 𝔸ℂ1×ℂ∗{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, hence ML⁡(A)=ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(A)={\mathbb{C}} (see Example 2.8 in [FZ2]), which contradicts our assumption. Clearly, the constant factor above is equal to ±1\pm 1 as soon as both δ\delta and ∂0{\partial}_{0} generate effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions.

Assume now that l>0l>0. By Lemma 3.6(d) we find a locally nilpotent derivation ∂′{\partial}^{\prime} with [δ~,∂′]=∂l[{\tilde{\delta}},{\partial}^{\prime}]={\partial}_{l}, and so by Lemma 3.6(c)

exp(∂′)δ~exp(−∂′)=δ~−[δ~,∂′]=δ~−∂l.\exp({\partial}^{\prime}){\tilde{\delta}}\exp(-{\partial}^{\prime})={\tilde{\delta}}-[{\tilde{\delta}},{\partial}^{\prime}]={\tilde{\delta}}-{\partial}_{l}.

Thus δ~−∂l{\tilde{\delta}}-{\partial}_{l} is again semisimple and its homogeneous components have degrees ≤l−1\leq l-1. Applying the induction hypothesis, the result follows. ∎

4. Toric surfaces and uniqueness of a DPD-presentation

4.1.

Let AA be a normal 2-dimensional ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-algebra with a grading A=⨁i∈ℤAiA=\bigoplus_{i\in{\mathbb{Z}}}A_{i} associated to an effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action. We recall that such a grading admits a DPD-presentation as follows (see [FZ1]).

Elliptic case: Here A0=ℂA_{0}={\mathbb{C}}, and up to switching the grading we have A−:=⨁i<0Ai=0A_{-}:=\bigoplus_{i<0}A_{i}=0. The curve C:=Proj⁡AC:=\operatorname{Proj}A is normal and carries a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-divisor DD of positive degree unique up to linear equivalence such that

(5) A=A0​[D]:=⨁i≥0H0​(C,𝒪C​(⌊i​D⌋))​ui⊆Frac⁡(C)​[u].\displaystyle A=A_{0}[D]:=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}H^{0}(C,{\mathcal{O}}_{C}(\lfloor iD\rfloor))u^{i}\subseteq\operatorname{Frac}(C)[u]\,.

Parabolic case: Here A−=0A_{-}=0, but A0A_{0} is 1-dimensional and so defines a smooth curve Spec⁡A0=Proj⁡A\operatorname{Spec}A_{0}=\operatorname{Proj}A. As before CC carries a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-divisor DD, now of arbitrary degree and again unique up to linear equivalence such that (5) holds.

Hyperbolic case: This case is characterized by A+,A−≠0A_{+},A_{-}\neq 0. The subrings A≥0:=⨁i≥0AiA_{\geq 0}:=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}A_{i} and A≤0A_{\leq 0} are parabolic and as before admit presentations A≥0=A0​[D+]⊆Frac⁡(C)​[u]A_{\geq 0}=A_{0}[D_{+}]\subseteq\operatorname{Frac}(C)[u] and A≤0=A0​[D−]⊆Frac⁡(C)​[u−1]A_{\leq 0}=A_{0}[D_{-}]\subseteq\operatorname{Frac}(C)[u^{-1}], respectively. Thus AA is the subring

The question arises whether a DPD-presentation is determined uniquely, up to the linear equivalence as above, an automorphism of CC and in the hyperbolic case by an interchange of D+D_{+} and D−D_{-}, by the geometry of the surface VV alone, disregarding the choice of a ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action. In Corollary 4.3 below we show that, indeed, this is the case at least for surfaces with a non-trivial Makar-Limanov invariant.

4.2.

Let us recall [FZ2, Theorem 4.5] that the Makar-Limanov invariant of a surface V=Spec⁡(A)V=\operatorname{Spec}(A), where A=A0​[D+,D−]A=A_{0}[D_{+},D_{-}] with D++D−≤0D_{+}+D_{-}\leq 0 and D++D−≠0D_{+}+D_{-}\neq 0, is trivial if and only if A0≅ℂ⁡[t]A_{0}\cong{\mathbb{C}}[t] and the fractional parts {D±}\{D_{\pm}\} of D±D_{\pm} are zero or are concentrated at one point, say, p±∈𝔸ℂ1p_{\pm}\in{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{1}. From Theorem 3.3 above and Theorem 4.3 in [FZ1] we derive the following corollary.

Corollary 4.3.

For a non-toric normal affine surface V=Spec⁡(A)V=\operatorname{Spec}(A) the following hold.

    If VV admits an effective elliptic ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action then this ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action is unique up to the automorphism λ⟼λ−1\lambda\longmapsto\lambda^{-1} of ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}. In particular a DPD-presentation A=A0​[D]A=A_{0}[D] is unique up to linear equivalence of DD.

Moreover, if A=A0​[D]=A0′​[D′]A=A_{0}[D]=A^{\prime}_{0}[D^{\prime}] are DPD-presentations corresponding to two ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions then there is an isomorphism φ:C→C′\varphi:C\to C^{\prime} of the curves defined by A0A_{0} and A0′A_{0}^{\prime}, respectively, such that DD and φ∗​(D′)\varphi^{*}(D^{\prime}) are linearly equivalent.

    are DPD-presentations of AA corresponding to two hyperbolic ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on AA then there is an isomorphism φ:A0→A0′\varphi:A_{0}\to A_{0}^{\prime} such that the pair of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-divisors (D+,D−)(D_{+},D_{-}) on the curve C=Spec⁡(A0)C=\operatorname{Spec}(A_{0}) is linearly equivalent to one of the pairs φ∗​(D+′,D−′)\varphi^{*}(D_{+}^{\prime},D_{-}^{\prime}) or φ∗​(D−′,D+′)\varphi^{*}(D_{-}^{\prime},D_{+}^{\prime}).

Proof.

If in case (a) there is a second ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action on AA not related to the first one by an automorphism of ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} then by Lemma 3.1 there is a locally nilpotent derivation on AA and so by Theorem 3.3 in [FZ2] VV is toric contrary to our assumption.

(b) and (c) follow immediately from the fact that any two ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on VV are conjugate in Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) by Theorem 3.3. ∎

Every 1-dimensional subgroup of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} isomorphic to ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} provides a ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action on VV. Conversely we have the following result.

Theorem 4.5.

If V=Spec⁡(A)V=\operatorname{Spec}(A) is an affine toric surface and if ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} acts effectively on VV then this action is conjugate to the action of a subtorus of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}.

Proof.

In the case V=𝕋V={\mathbb{T}} this is evident. So we can assume in the sequel that V≠𝕋V\neq{\mathbb{T}}. This ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action then defines a grading A=⨁i∈ZAiA=\bigoplus_{i\in Z}A_{i} of AA. [FZ2, Theorem 3.16]). By Proposition 3.8 in [FZ1] this would imply that VV has at least two singular points, which is impossible.

(−e+d+​[p],e−d−​[p]).\left(-\frac{e_{+}}{d_{+}}[p],\frac{e_{-}}{d_{-}}[p]\right)\,.

As a particular case we obtain the following classical result.

Corollary 4.6.

(Gutwirth [Gut]) Every ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action on 𝔸ℂ2{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{C}}^{2} is linearizable.

Remarks 4.7.

1. Any two effective actions of a 2-torus on a normal affine surface VV are conjugate. This follows from the fact that any toric surface is equivariantly isomorphic to one of the surfaces ℂ∗2{\mathbb{C}}^{*2}, 𝔸ℂ1×ℂ∗{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*} or Vd,eV_{d,e}, and two such surfaces are isomorphic as abstract surfaces if and only if (6) holds.

2. Every normal affine surface V=Spec⁡(A)V=\operatorname{Spec}(A) with an elliptic or parabolic ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-action and with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant is toric (see Theorems 3.3 and 3.14 in [FZ2]). This yields that there can be at most one parabolic DPD-presentation A=A0​[D]A=A_{0}[D] on an affine normal surface, up to the equivalence described in Corollary 4.3(b).

5. Homogeneous affine surfaces

In this section we show the following result.

Theorem 5.1.

Let VV be one of the surfaces ℙ1×ℙ1\Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta or ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q, where Δ\Delta is the diagonal in ℙ1×ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and QQ is a nonsingular quadric in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. In case V=ℙ2\QV={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q this is a result of [DG], see also [Do]. This theorem follows immediately from the following two more general statements.

Every smooth Gorenstein ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-surface V=Spec⁡(A)V=\operatorname{Spec}(A) with Cl⁡(V)≅ℤ\operatorname{Cl}(V)\cong{\mathbb{Z}} and ML⁡(V)=ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(V)={\mathbb{C}} is isomorphic to V≅ℙ1×ℙ1\ΔV\cong{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta, where Δ\Delta is the diagonal. l=card​{p∈𝔸ℂ1:D+​(p)+D−​(p)<0}=2.l=\mbox{card}\ \{p\in{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}:D_{+}(p)+D_{-}(p)<0\}=2.

Proposition 5.3.

A smooth ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-surface V=Spec⁡AV=\operatorname{Spec}A with Pic⁡(V)≅ℤ2\operatorname{Pic}(V)\cong{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} and ML⁡(V)=ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(V)={\mathbb{C}} is isomorphic to ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q, where QQ is a smooth quadric in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. Remark 5.4.

If a torus of dimension kk acts effectively on a variety VV of dimension nn, then k≤nk\leq n. Thus the rank of a reductive group GG acting effectively on VV is bounded by nn. As every increasing chain of connected reductive groups with bounded rank becomes stationary, this shows the following fact: every connected reductive subgroup of Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) is contained in a maximal one.

In the Introduction we posed the question whether any two maximal connected reductive subgroups of the automorphism group of a normal affine surface are conjugate. We note that this would follow if one could prove that

(∗)(*) any two effective ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-actions on a non-toric surface VV with ML⁡(V)=ℂ{\operatorname{ML}}(V)={\mathbb{C}} are conjugate.

In fact, if VV admits no 𝐒𝐋2{\bf{SL}}_{2}-action then every maximal connected reductive subgroup of Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) is a torus. In this case the result follows from (∗)(*), Theorems 3.3, 4.5 and Remark 4.7(1).

If VV admits an action of 𝐒𝐋2{\bf{SL}}_{2} then by the Theorem of Gizatullin and Popov mentioned in the Introduction VV is one of the surfaces ℙ1×ℙ1\Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta, ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q, or Vd,1V_{d,1} (d≥1d\geq 1).

If VV is one of the surfaces ℙ1×ℙ1\Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta or ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q then the standard actions of 𝐏𝐆𝐋2{\bf PGL}_{2} on VV cannot be extended to a larger connected reductive group, since otherwise there would be an action of a 2-torus on VV. Thus in these cases the maximal connected reductive subgroups of Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) are isomorphic to 𝐏𝐆𝐋2{\bf PGL}_{2} and, moreover, any two such subgroups are conjugate in Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) by Proposition 4.14 in [FZ2].

Similarly, if V=Vd,1V=V_{d,1} then 𝐆𝐋2/ℤd{\bf{GL}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{d} is a maximal connected reductive subgroup of Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V). Given another maximal connected reductive subgroup GG of Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) we may suppose by Remark 4.7(1) that its maximal torus is equal to the standard one in 𝐆𝐋2/ℤd{\bf{GL}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{d}. Now it is easy to see that GG and 𝐆𝐋2/ℤd{\bf{GL}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{d} are equal (alternatively one can apply Lemma 4.17 in [FZ2]).

From this remark and Theorems 3.3, 4.5 and 5.1 we deduce the following corollary.

Corollary 5.5.

For a normal affine surface VV, any two maximal connected reductive subgroups of the automorphism group Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) are conjugate in Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) except possibly in the case where VV is non-toric, has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant and is not isomorphic to one of the surfaces ℙ1×ℙ1\Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\backslash\Delta or ℙ2\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\backslash Q.

The forthcoming paper [FKZ] will be devoted to this remaining case.

Added in proofs. We are grateful to Peter Russell who showed us an example, given any k≥2k\geq 2, of a non-toric smooth affine surface with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant that admits kk mutually non-conjugated ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}-subgroups in the automorphism group. This gives, in general, a negative answer to the question in the Introduction. Such a surface appears as the complement in a Hirzebruch surface of a section with selfintersection number k+1k+1. These surfaces were studied in [DG, II].

We are also grateful to Jürgen Hausen who informed us, after appearing of the first e-print version of this paper, that in [BeHau] an nn-dimensional generalization of our Theorem 4.5 had been proven. Namely, it was shown that an effective action of the torus 𝕋n−1{\mathbb{T}}^{n-1} on an nn-dimensional affine toric variety VV is conjugate in the automorphism group Aut⁡(V){\operatorname{Aut}}(V) to a subgroup of the standard action of 𝕋n{\mathbb{T}}^{n} on VV.
